evidence.note: Periodically runs the workspace suite, greps 'test result:' and counts compile errors ('only 3 errors, down from many'), establishing a rough baseline of passing vs remaining.

Consolidates a list of failing test binaries ('19 test files failing to compile with ~116 unique errors') while confirming common 34/34 — a coarse done-vs-remaining ledger, but only compile-status, not per-binary pass counts.

Maintains a repeated status header (Workspace builds ✅, common 34/34 ✅, ~13 test files fail to compile) and tracks the failing-compile count declining from ~19 to ~13; re-verifies common after edits (regression check on the shared crate).
Explicitly detects circular debugging ('We've been going in circles with sed corruption of resources.rs') — a level-8 trait of recognizing thrashing.

Despite naming the loop, the agent repeats the same restore-backup-and-re-corrupt cycle for hundreds of steps to the end (step 504), never escaping and never reaching a workspace pass count — thrash-detection did not produce reprioritization; fixed work is repeated across the long horizon.

reasoning: The agent periodically runs the suite, works down a list of failing crates, and roughly tracks remaining work via a repeated status header and compile-error counts (anchor 5), and it does verbally detect circular debugging (an anchor-8 trait). But it never maintained per-binary pass counts across the 100 binaries (they never compiled) and — decisively — its detection of thrashing produced no effective reprioritization: it repeated the same corrupting restore/fix cycle for a large fraction of the horizon, i.e. it kept repeating fixed work. That combination of genuine-but-coarse tracking with un-acted-upon thrash awareness lands solidly at 5, short of the sustained, self-correcting accounting the higher anchors require.
